<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Efficiently solving real-world problems with LLMs increasingly hinges on their ability to interact with dynamic web environments and autonomously acquire external information. While recent research like Search-R1 and WebDancer demonstrates strong performance in solving web tasks, they heavily rely on additional tools to convert the interactive web environment into static text content. This is in contrast to human browsing behaviors, which involve diverse interactions with the browser, such as scrolling, clicking, and typing. In this paper, we propose BrowserAgent, a more interactive agent that solves complex tasks through human-inspired browser actions. BrowserAgent operates directly on raw web pages via Playwright through a set of predefined browser actions. We adopt a two-stage training (Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Rejection Fine-Tuning (RFT)) to improve the model’s generalization abilities. Despite using significantly less training data than Search-R1, BrowserAgent achieves more competitive results across different Open-QA tasks. Additionally, we introduce an explicit memory mechanism to store key conclusions across steps, further enhancing the model’s reasoning capabilities for long-horizon tasks. Notably, BrowserAgent-7B can achieve around 20% improvement over Search-R1 on multi-hop QA tasks like HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and Bamboogle. These results indicate that BrowserAgent can serve as a more advanced framework for more interactive and scalable web agents.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

</table>
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2510.10666v2/com1.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:532/183;" width="532" height="183" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Evaluation Result of the Browseragent.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Web agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lieberman et al., 1995</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>)</cite> are autonomous systems that can interact with vast amounts of web information to make decisions and take actions to accomplish complex real-world tasks. It has been a long-standing research field to study how to automate the complex information-seeking process. Recently, Deep Research Agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite> from ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini demonstrated that current LLMs exhibit unprecedented abilities to solve highly complex real-world tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mialon et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Following these commercialized deep research systems, there has been a surging interest in the open-source community to replicate their promising results. For example,  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2025c)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al. (2025a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025a)</a></cite> have attempted various forms of SFT and RL approaches to post-train LLMs into web agents. However, these frameworks rely heavily on external tools like HTML-parser (e.g., Jina service) and summarizers (e.g., prompting GPT-4o to summarize the web page) to turn dynamic web information into static short-length documents. This will <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) restrict the agents’ abilities to interact with web pages to acquire in-depth information, and (2) incur a very high cost due to calling the additional tools.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2510.10666v2/diff.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/188;" width="494" height="188" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Comparison Between BrowserAgent and Traditional Deep Research Pipeline.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, humans exhibit highly interactive browsing behaviors when solving complex web tasks. For example, Humans perform actions like hyperlink clicking, form typing, and scrolling up/down through the browser to navigate through the web for information gathering. This allows humans to acquire more in-depth and native knowledge from the web without relying on additional summarization services. Inspired by this, we resort to browser automation frameworks like Playwright to enable these interactions with dynamic DOM elements, allowing LLM agents to share the same representation space and action set as humans do.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While browser-based agents enable rich interaction, prior works such as AssistantBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoran et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite> primarily used them as evaluation-only benchmarks, because Playwright cannot be efficiently parallelized. This results in extremely low throughput ( 1–2 episodes/minute), making large-scale training infeasible. To overcome this, we develop a Ray-parallelized orchestration layer that scales to dozens of Playwright instances. On a single 32-core server, our system achieves 50+ episodes/minute, reducing the cost of browser-native data collection by over an order of magnitude (see Section <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Environment Setting ‣ 2 browseragent ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a> for more details). Building on this infrastructure, we explore strategies for constructing high-quality, behaviorally rich training datasets directly from live browser sessions. In contrast to methods that passively snapshot every intermediate state, our system selectively maintains a structured historical memory of key conclusions while prioritizing the current observation context—balancing long-term reasoning with real-time perception. This improves both sample efficiency and downstream agent performance. A vivid comparison is depicted in <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We build <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BrowserAgent</span>—a scalable, end-to-end browser-native agent framework that learns directly from real-time web interactions rather than relying on static content abstraction. BrowserAgent offers several advantages over prior work: It defines a minimal yet expressive set of atomic browser operations—such as scrolling, clicking, typing, and tab management—that closely align with real human behavior on the web. Rather than relying on LLM-based semantic abstractions, BrowserAgent interacts directly with raw webpage states, enabling fine-grained and compositional decision-making.
BrowserAgent also departs from complex reinforcement learning strategies, instead using a lightweight two-stage training pipeline of SFT followed by rejection sampling. This simple yet effective approach achieves strong performance—especially in multi-hop reasoning tasks—while requiring less data and infrastructure. Furthermore, its iterative ReAct-style reasoning framework, enhanced with explicit memory, empowers the agent to perform multi-turn interactions and complex inference across information sources. With only 5.3K training samples, BrowserAgent can already demonstrate strong generalization and robustness. Our model can outperform Search-R1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> significantly on a wide range of Open-QA tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Through these experimental results, we demonstrate that BrowserAgent can serve as a good alternative approach to existing frameworks. Our work sheds light on how to build more scalable and interactive web agents for solving complex web tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>browseragent</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present the detailed design of the BrowserAgent training methodology. This includes: (1) <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">defining a minimal yet expressive set of atomic browser operations to generate high-quality training data through interaction with dynamic web environments, ensuring that the agent learns how to engage with real-world web content;</span> and (2) <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">training BrowserAgent using efficient SFT and RFT to enable it to handle complex reasoning tasks.</span> Our approach focuses on leveraging real-time web interaction instead of relying on static datasets, providing a more flexible and scalable training framework. By systematically generating data from interactive search behaviors, we have successfully enhanced the model’s problem-solving capabilities and its ability to handle diverse, real-world information.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2510.10666v2/test_3.png" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/439;" width="548" height="439" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Overview of the Browseragent framework.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Framework Design</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">First, we simulate real human operations by defining four categories of actions: <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">page operation actions</span>, <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">tab management actions</span>, <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">URL navigation actions</span>, and <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">completion actions</span>. The BrowserAgent action categories and their corresponding command descriptions are provided in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.1 Framework Design ‣ 2 browseragent ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. These categories are designed to comprehensively cover the full spectrum of human–web interaction behaviors. Unlike other approaches, we do not rely on any additional models for web parsing and summarization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Instead, we simulate human browsing behavior through direct interactions with the web page—such as scroll up/down actions in the page operation category—enabling the model to gradually develop the ability to autonomously locate required information and understand web content during training. This design brings multiple advantages. Fine-grained page operation and tab management actions not only enhance the model’s understanding of web structures and its adaptability to multi-task scenarios, but also significantly improve the agent’s generalization ability in complex web environments. Furthermore, by simulating human exploratory behaviors through actions like scroll up/down, the model is compelled to actively filter, locate, and integrate key information during real interactions. This avoids shortcuts such as relying on an additional large model for summarization, and gradually builds the model’s capabilities in information retrieval, reading comprehension, and content integration throughout the training process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">we simulate human search behavior through an iterative cycle of thinking–summarizing–acting.</span> Conceptually, this paradigm can be regarded as a variant of the ReAct framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023b</a>)</cite> augmented with a memory module, enabling the agent to maintain contextual continuity across multiple interaction turns. Specifically, both data generation and model inference are conducted through our automated multi-turn interaction process. We provide the system prompt and question, interact with the server to obtain observations, and then provide the prompt, question, and observations to GPT-4.1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024</a>)</cite>, which outputs the (reasoning, action) pairs like ReAct  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>. Additionally, we require the model to record necessary conclusions. This process is iterated until the model outputs an answer to the question or the number of steps exceeds the limit. We keep track of historical actions and conclusions as memory in the input to help the model understand the completed actions and gather necessary information. The complete workflow is outlined in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.4 Training ‣ 2 browseragent ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The prompt is provided in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 System Prompt ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Dataset Synthesis</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To equip the model with comprehensive problem-solving capabilities, we selected the general question answering dataset NQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwiatkowski et al., 2019</a>)</cite> and the multi-hop question answering dataset HotpotQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. These two datasets cover basic factual questions and tasks that require complex reasoning and multi-step inference, helping the model learn richer reasoning paths and answering strategies in different types of problem scenarios. Our dataset consists of a total of 5.3K high-quality trajetories. Among them, 4K routes come from NQ and HotpotQA for simple question-answering tasks. The rest 1.3K trajetories are selected from HotpotQA to specifically improve the model’s ability to tackle complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. All selected samples are processed through our automated multi-turn interaction collection process. The detailed procedure is described in Section <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Framework Design ‣ 2 browseragent ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For basic capability data, the system drives the large model to interact with the web environment for up to 6 steps, and for challenging data, it drives the large model to interact with the web environment for up to 30 steps. Every step is fully recorded, including the input prompt, model output, current page observation, and intermediate conclusions. This process ultimately generates detailed reasoning and decision-making trajectory data. Our case is provided in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Case Study ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>. Through this dual selection and collection strategy, our dataset not only ensures broad coverage of the model’s basic capabilities but also specifically enhances its performance in complex, multi-hop reasoning scenarios, laying a solid foundation for subsequent agent training and evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Environment Setting</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on Verl-Tool <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we implement a playwright-based tool to mimic the interaction with the browser. The observation is pure text-based, as an accessibility tree parsed by Playwright <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Microsoft, 2020</a>)</cite> (see example in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2 browseragent ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). To improve page readability, we do some rule-based post-processing such as merging consecutive text elements on the accessibility tree. To deploy Wikipedia <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karpukhin et al., 2020</a>)</cite> locally, we adopt the offline Kiwix version with content updated to 2022. To standardize the interface and accelerate interactions, we employed the Verl-Tool framework with a Ray-based <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moritz et al., 2018</a>)</cite> tool server as the top-level interface. All requests were routed through FastAPI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramírez, 2018</a>)</cite>, enabling uniform scheduling by the backend. Based on the design of Verl-Tool’s tool server, each episode is assigned a unique trace_id to maintain the correspondence with its browser session, and the session is automatically terminated once a stop action is received. In our experiments, we deployed 64 concurrent Playwright browsers on a single machine with 32-CPUs. While the top-level scheduling is orchestrated by Ray <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moritz et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, the framework exhibits strong potential for scaling to much larger CPU clusters.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Training</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To enhance the model’s ability to generate high-quality, structured answers, we propose a two-stage training framework comprising SFT and RFT, as illustrated in the Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2 browseragent ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage 1: SFT.</span> In the first stage, we perform SFT on the base model Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using 5.3K question-answer pairs generated via the method described in Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Dataset Synthesis ‣ 2 browseragent ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>. This stage is designed to teach the model the desired answer format and to equip it with basic reasoning capabilities. The model is trained until convergence, and the checkpoint with the best evaluation loss is selected as the final SFT model. The evaluation loss curve is shown in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Eval Loss Curve ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>. The primary goal of the SFT stage is to establish an initial understanding of the answer structure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage 2: RFT with Reasoning Path Selection.</span> In the second stage, we leverage the SFT model obtained from the first stage to construct training data for reinforced fine-tuning. Specifically, for each question in the training sets of NQ and HotpotQA, we sample four answers from the SFT model. We then use the EM metric for filtering, following the approach in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiong et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, to select instances where the model-generated answers include both correct and incorrect responses among the four candidates. From these instances, we choose the correct answer that contains the largest number of reasoning steps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, as more reasoning steps indicate deeper model thinking. This encourages the model to learn richer and more in-depth reasoning patterns. The selected samples constitute our Original RFT Data. To preserve the distributional characteristics of the original data and mitigate the issue of catastrophic forgetting of the answer format learned during the SFT stage, we randomly sample a portion of the SFT data and combine it with the filtered Original RFT Data to construct the final dataset used in the second-stage training. We then further fine-tune the SFT model on this mixed dataset, thereby enhancing its reasoning capability while maintaining its ability to generate well-structured answers. The specific data ratio and filtering strategy are detailed in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 filtering strategy and data ratio ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To comprehensively evaluate the performance of Browseragent, we selected six representative benchmark datasets, which are divided into two categories: The first category is general question answering datasets, including NQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwiatkowski et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, and PopQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mallen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>; the second category is multi-hop question answering datasets, including HotpotQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, 2WikiMultiHopQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, Musique <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and Bamboogle <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Press et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. These datasets encompass a diverse range of search and reasoning tasks, enabling a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of Browseragent.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Evaluation Metrics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In our experiments, we adopted two evaluation methods: <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">exact match (EM)</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM-based judgment</span>. EM offers an objective measure of consistency between model outputs and ground truth, but often underestimates performance when answers are factually correct and semantically reasonable yet differ in surface form (see case study in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Case Study ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>). To complement this, we introduced an LLM-based judgment mechanism: each model-generated answer was independently evaluated by GPT-4.1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024</a>)</cite>, Gemini Flash 2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepMind, 2023</a>)</cite>, and Claude Sonnet 3.7 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2024</a>)</cite>, and classified as “valid” if at least two judged it correct. By combining EM with consensus voting among multiple LLMs, our framework provides a more comprehensive and reliable view of model performance, mitigating the limitations of single-metric evaluation in complex, open-domain QA tasks. The full evaluation prompt is provided in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Evaluation Prompt ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Baselines</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the effectiveness of BrowserAgent, we compared it with the following baseline methods, adopting the same settings as those used in Search-R1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>:
(1) Inference without Retrieval: Direct inference and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. (2) Inference with Retrieval: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lewis et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, IRCoT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and Search-o1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025d</a>)</cite>. (3) Fine
Tuning-Based Methods: SFT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chung et al., 2022</a>)</cite>;
(4) RL-based methods: Search-R1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These baselines cover a broad range of paradigms in retrieval augmentation and fine-tuning, providing a representative comparison for evaluating BrowserAgent. For fairness, we use the same pre-trained LLM across all methods and align the training data sources with those of the baselines. Although our training scale is much smaller than those used in prior work, BrowserAgent still achieves non-trivial performance gains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct our experiments using the Qwen2.5-7b-Instruct model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2024</a>)</cite>. The 2022 Wikipedia dump <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karpukhin et al., 2020</a>)</cite> is used as the knowledge source. During evaluation, we limit the model to a maximum of 30 rounds of browser interactions. Other training details can be found in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS6" title="B.6 Experimental Setup ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Experimental Results</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the experimental results in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.5 Experimental Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we find that BrowserAgent consistently outperforms strong baselines across a range of tasks, demonstrating robust performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluations. Our RFT stage achieves consistent improvements over the SFT stage, particularly on multi-hop QA tasks. Notably, BrowserAgent significantly outperforms multiple versions of Search-R1. Specifically, BrowserAgent-7B can achieve around a <span id="S3.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">20%</span> improvement over Search-R1-Instruct on multi-hop QA tasks. This advantage stems from its ability to handle longer reasoning chains without being constrained by context length. Even with limited training data and only a simple, efficient RFT strategy, it still outperforms Search-R1-Instruct trained with complex reinforcement learning techniques, fully demonstrating the effectiveness and practicality of BrowserAgent’s end-to-end paradigm based on direct interaction with web pages in tasks involving active web exploration and complex reasoning. Moreover, as RFT does not use explicit format-based rewards, EM alone may not fully capture performance; incorporating LLM-based judgment provides a more comprehensive evaluation of the model’s true capabilities.</p>
</div>

</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.6 </span>Ablation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the ablation studies, we randomly sampled 1K examples from each benchmark dataset for evaluation. As Bamboogle contains fewer than 1,000 instances, we evaluated it in full. Since RFT models trained on poorly performing SFT models tend to exhibit even lower performance, we conducted most ablation experiments on the SFT model, while using the RFT model specifically for step-wise ablations. In this section, we report only the EM scores as the evaluation metric.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Increasing Memory Capacity.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For instance, when answering a question like “Who is the father of the greatest NBA player of all time?”, the model may first determine that “Michael Jordan is the greatest NBA player” and then retrieve that “Jordan’s father is James Jordan.” Without storing the intermediate conclusion, the model risks losing the connection to the original question and falling into a circular search pattern. To enhance reasoning efficiency and avoid redundant steps, we increased the model’s memory capacity by training it to summarize and retain intermediate conclusions during multi-hop reasoning. The experimental results in Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Increasing Memory Capacity. ‣ 3.6 Ablation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> show that the proposed method not only effectively prevents information loss and logical disconnection in reasoning chains, but also improves the model’s overall performance and generalization when handling complex tasks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Results of the Ablation Study on BrowserAgent-SFT.</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multi-round observation v.s. Single-round observation</h5>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Previous argentic posttraining works such as RAGEN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Search-R1 treat the entire tool-use trajectory as a single input, appending all retrieved content and intermediate reasoning steps into the context. This approach is limited by the context window, restricting scalability during inference. To address this, we introduce a memory mechanism that stores only key conclusions in a structured &lt;memory&gt; format, removing redundant context while preserving essential information. This enables the model to reason more efficiently and scale to up to 30 reasoning steps without exceeding context limits. The experimental results in Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Increasing Memory Capacity. ‣ 3.6 Ablation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> demonstrate that trimming redundant input not only improves model performance, but also enhances its scalability in handling complex multi-hop tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Model Size Scaling</h5>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to computational resource constraints, we conducted comparative experiments using models with 3B and 7B parameters. As shown in the Table <a href="#S3.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Increasing Memory Capacity. ‣ 3.6 Ablation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the 7B model consistently outperforms the 3B model across all evaluation benchmarks, demonstrating stronger reasoning capabilities and better generalization. This result provides compelling evidence for the importance of scaling model size in multi-hop reasoning and complex question answering tasks. Furthermore, it highlights that even under limited training data and relatively lightweight fine-tuning procedures, model capacity remains a critical factor influencing overall performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Test Step Scaling</h5>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Leveraging our single-turn context window architecture, the proposed method scales effectively by increasing the number of interaction rounds. While performance is slightly lower than Search-R1 at around 6 turns, it improves steadily as the number of turns grows. Notably, even with a significantly increased maximum step limit (e.g., 30 steps), the average number of reasoning steps remains stable, indicating the model’s ability to complete tasks efficiently without overusing the step budget. The detailed experimental results can be found in Tables <a href="#A2.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ B.7.1 Test Step Scaling ‣ B.7 Experimental Results ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#A2.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ B.7.1 Test Step Scaling ‣ B.7 Experimental Results ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS7.SSS1" title="B.7.1 Test Step Scaling ‣ B.7 Experimental Results ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.7.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Rejection sampling Fine-Tuning</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2023</a>)</cite> is a widely adopted strategy for enhancing large language models (LLMs), particularly when integrating generative models with external evaluation criteria or retrieval mechanisms. In this approach, the model generates multiple candidate outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> for each input. These candidates are then assessed using predefined evaluation metrics—such as answer correctness or adherence to specific constraints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Only the top-performing responses, as determined by the evaluation criteria, are retained through rejection sampling. The resulting high-quality samples are subsequently used to further fine-tune the model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. This method has been shown to effectively improve the accuracy and robustness of LLMs across various tasks, including question answering, code generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, and reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2025</a>)</cite>. We extend this method to the domain of browser agents and achieve strong performance on several key tasks, demonstrating its broad applicability and effectiveness in dynamic web environments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Agentic Information Seeking</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Agentic Information Seeking is a retrieval approach in which an agent actively participates in acquiring and integrating information. Unlike traditional keyword search, this method allows the agent to behave like a human user, automatically performing a series of operations in a browser or web environment—such as typing, clicking, and navigating—to progressively collect and filter useful information. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">de Chezelles et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nakano et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schick et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Murphy et al., 2025</a>)</cite> It is typically powered by large language models or automation strategies, enabling the agent to understand complex tasks, dynamically adjust its actions, and synthesize information from multiple sources to meet complex or multi-turn information needs.
Although current approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> make notable progress in this field, they still face several limitations—for instance, their limited capacity to model long-context information, which results in a heavy reliance on external resources such as the Jina service and larger-scale pretrained models. To address these challenges, we propose a strategy that integrates web page scrolling operations (e.g., scroll up and down) into an end-to-end model, enabling the agent to actively read web content. This approach effectively alleviates the issues above and enables efficient understanding of complex web information.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Agentic Search</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Web Agents are intelligent agent systems capable of autonomously interacting with internet resources <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025e</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, such as web pages and search engines, to accomplish complex tasks including multi-step reasoning, information retrieval, question answering, and data integration. Typically, these systems leverage LLMs as their decision-making core, in combination with tool invocation, web page parsing, retrieval, and automated execution functionalities. In recent years, Web Agents have become a critical foundation for research in open-domain problem solving, retrieval-augmented generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, AI assistants, and automated search-based reasoning. Recent works mainly focus on benchmarking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoran et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> rather than training agents directly in these environments, primarily because browser-based interaction is computationally expensive. To this end, we have implemented an efficient and easy-to-use two-stage browser agent training pipeline, which ensures scalability while significantly reducing the system overhead of environment interactions, thereby laying the foundation for large-scale autonomous learning of Web Agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper presents BrowserAgent, an efficient and scalable training framework for real-world web interaction. Unlike previous approaches that rely on static summaries or external parsing services, our method leverages Playwright to enable end-to-end web operations, allowing the model to actively acquire and integrate information through fine-grained actions such as scrolling and clicking. Combined with a parallel tool serving architecture and an explicit memory mechanism, our two-stage SFT + RFT training strategy reduces redundant context while enabling efficient scaling along complex reasoning chains. Experimental and ablation results demonstrate that BrowserAgent achieves significant advantages in performance, scalability, and data efficiency. Notably, BrowserAgent outperforms existing methods (e.g., Search-R1) using a smaller amount of training data, especially excelling in multi-hop reasoning tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In future work, we plan to explore more intelligent memory mechanisms, cross-website generalization, multi-agent collaboration, and continual learning from interaction logs to advance BrowserAgent toward a truly general-purpose web agent.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Ethics Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This study does not involve any personal data, sensitive information, or high-risk application scenarios. No ethically controversial datasets or models were used. All experimental data are standard benchmark datasets that are publicly available, and the sole purpose of this research is to advance the development of web-based agent systems. Therefore, we believe this work does not pose any significant ethical risks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Reproducibility Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure the reproducibility of our experiments, we have provided the complete implementation code in the supplementary materials. All technical details, including the evaluation benchmarks, baseline methods, and training hyperparameter settings used in this work, can be found in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Experiments ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>The Usage of LLMs</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this study, we use LLMs for data generation, result evaluation in the experiments. For the paper writing, we use LLMs for paper polishing, generating visualizations like figures, and retrieving related work. We have proofread carefully to ensure no hallucinated content in the paper.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Evaluation Prompt</h3>

<figure id="A2.SS2.fig1" class="ltx_figure"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.SS2.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="135.13" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 135.13" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,135.13) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#666666;" fill="#666666" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 8.91 L 0 126.21 C 0 131.14 3.99 135.13 8.91 135.13 L 541.09 135.13 C 546.01 135.13 550 131.14 550 126.21 L 550 8.91 C 550 3.99 546.01 0 541.09 0 L 8.91 0 C 3.99 0 0 3.99 0 8.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F9F9F9;" fill="#F9F9F9" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.04 8.91 L 1.04 112.88 L 548.96 112.88 L 548.96 8.91 C 548.96 4.56 545.44 1.04 541.09 1.04 L 8.91 1.04 C 4.56 1.04 1.04 4.56 1.04 8.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 8.91 120.54)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:33.44em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="462.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">

Given a question, its corresponding ground truth, and an answer, you need to decide whether the answer is correct. If it is correct, please output "yes" otherwise output "no".</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS2.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">question: {}</span></span>

<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>System Prompt</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="1065.13" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 1065.13" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,1065.13) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#666666;" fill="#666666" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 9.26 L 0 1055.87 C 0 1060.98 4.14 1065.13 9.26 1065.13 L 540.74 1065.13 C 545.86 1065.13 550 1060.98 550 1055.87 L 550 9.26 C 550 4.14 545.86 0 540.74 0 L 9.26 0 C 4.14 0 0 4.14 0 9.26 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F9F9F9;" fill="#F9F9F9" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.38 9.26 L 1.38 1042.3 L 548.62 1042.3 L 548.62 9.26 C 548.62 4.91 545.09 1.38 540.74 1.38 L 9.26 1.38 C 4.91 1.38 1.38 4.91 1.38 9.26 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.26 1050.31)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:33.4em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.18" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.49)" width="462.16"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:33.4em;">
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Prompt</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.26 11.95)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:38.41em;--ltx-fo-height:73.9em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="1025.18" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 1022.49)" width="531.49"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:38.41em;">
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">You are a browser interaction assistant designed to execute step-by-step browser operations efficiently and precisely to complete the user’s task. You are provided with specific tasks and webpage-related information, and you need to output accurate actions to accomplish the user’s task.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Here’s the information you’ll have:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The user’s objective: This is the task you’re trying to complete.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The current web page’s accessibility tree: This is a simplified representation of the webpage, providing key information.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The open tabs: These are the tabs you have open.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The previous actions: There are the actions you just performed. It may be helpful to track your progress.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Information already found: Information related to the current query that has been identified in historical actions. You need to integrate and supplement this information.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The actions you can perform fall into several categories:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Page Operation Actions:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.10.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘click [id] [content]‘: This action clicks on an element with a specific id on the webpage.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.11" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.11.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘type [id] [content] [press_enter_after=0|1]‘: Use this to type the content into the field with id. By default, the ""Enter"" key is pressed after typing unless press_enter_after is set to 0.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.12" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.12.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘hover [id] [content]‘: Hover over an element with id.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.13" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.13.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘press [key_comb]‘: Simulates the pressing of a key combination on the keyboard (e.g., Ctrl+v).</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.14" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.14.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘scroll [down|up]‘: Scroll the page up or down.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.15" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.15.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Tab Management Actions:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.16" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.16.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘new_tab‘: Open a new, empty browser tab.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.17" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.17.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘tab_focus [tab_index]‘: Switch the browser’s focus to a specific tab using its index.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.18" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.18.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘close_tab‘: Close the currently active tab.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.19" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.19.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">URL Navigation Actions:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.20" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.20.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘goto [url]‘: Navigate to a specific URL.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.21" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.21.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘go_back‘: Navigate to the previously viewed page.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.22" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.22.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘go_forward‘: Navigate to the next page (if a previous ’go_back’ action was performed).</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.23" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.23.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Completion Action:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.24" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.24.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">‘stop [answer]‘: Issue this action when you believe the task is complete. If the objective is to find a text-based answer, provide the answer in the bracket. If you believe the task is impossible to complete, provide the answer as ""N/A"" in the bracket.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.25" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.25.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">To be successful, it is very important to follow the following rules:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.26" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.26.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">1. You should only issue an action that is valid given the current observation.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.27" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.27.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">2. You should only issue one action at a time.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.28" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.28.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">3. You should follow the examples to reason step by step and then issue the next action.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.29" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.29.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">4. You should refer to historical actions when issue an action and try not to make repetitive actions.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.30" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.30.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">5. All reasoning must be inside ‘&lt;think&gt;&lt;/think&gt;‘ tags, and there must be no output before ‘&lt;think&gt;&lt;/think&gt;‘.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.31" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.31.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">6. After ‘&lt;think&gt;&lt;/think&gt;‘, only the action should be generated in the correct format, enclosed in code fences. For example:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.32" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.32.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">&lt;think&gt;This button looks relevant to my goal. Clicking it should take me to the next step.&lt;/think&gt;</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.33" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.33.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">“‘click [id] [content]“‘</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.34" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.34.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">7. Issue the stop action when you think you have achieved the objective. Don’t generate anything after stop.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.35" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.35.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">8. Always format actions correctly:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.36" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.36.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">“‘command [parameters]“‘</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.37" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.37.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">For example, if searching for ""death row inmates in the US"" in a search field with ID ‘21‘, correctly format it as:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.38" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.38.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">“‘type [21] [death row inmates in the US] [1]“‘</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.39" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.39.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Avoid incorrect formats that omit brackets around parameters or numeric values.</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.40" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS3.p1.pic1.2.40.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">9.Between &lt;think&gt;&lt;/think&gt;, you need to use &lt;conclusion&gt;&lt;/conclusion&gt; to enclose the information obtained in this round that is relevant to the current query. Note that if there is no valid information, this part is not required. The enclosed information must be directly usable to answer the original query.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>Case Study</h3>

<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this case of the NQ dataset, our BrowserAgent uses 3 steps to interact with the web environment and find the final answer of the given question. The ground truth of the question is "Edward IV of England", but the BrowserAgent gives the final answer "King Edward IV". Obviously, these two are semantically equivalent, but we cannot use the EM method to match them.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="1589.36" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 1589.36" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,1589.36) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#666666;" fill="#666666" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 9.26 L 0 1580.1 C 0 1585.21 4.14 1589.36 9.26 1589.36 L 540.74 1589.36 C 545.86 1589.36 550 1585.21 550 1580.1 L 550 9.26 C 550 4.14 545.86 0 540.74 0 L 9.26 0 C 4.14 0 0 4.14 0 9.26 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F9F9F9;" fill="#F9F9F9" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.38 9.26 L 1.38 1566.42 L 548.62 1566.42 L 548.62 9.26 C 548.62 4.91 545.09 1.38 540.74 1.38 L 9.26 1.38 C 4.91 1.38 1.38 4.91 1.38 9.26 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.26 1574.43)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:33.4em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="462.16"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:33.4em;">
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Case Study</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.26 28.55)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:38.41em;--ltx-fo-height:110.57em;--ltx-fo-depth:1.39em;font-size:10pt;" height="1549.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 1530.01)" width="531.49"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:38.41em;">
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Question:<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Who was the father of the princes in the tower?</span></span></span>
</span>
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle" style="width:384.1pt;--ltx-bg-color:#B3B3B3;">
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 1</span></span>
</span></span></span>
</span>
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Input Sequence:<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span>
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p5.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">System prompt: …</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p5.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.pic1.p5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Observation:</span></span>

<p id="A2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this case of the HotpotQA dataset, our BrowserAgent uses 3 steps to interact with the web environment
and find the final answer of the given question. The ground truth of the question is "no", but the BrowserAgent gives the final answer "Skin Yard was from the U.S. (Seattle, Washington). Ostava was from Bulgaria (not the U.S.).". For this judgmental question, our agent provided a negative answer to prove that the two cities come from different countries, which is equivalent to a negative answer from the ground truth.</p>

It was formed in 1991…" and its origin is listed as Gabrovo, Bulgaria. Therefore, Ostava is not from the U.S., but from Bulgaria.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.15.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
</span></span>&lt;/think&gt;</span><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.15.2" class="ltx_text"></span></span>
<span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.16" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.16.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#D493DF;">&lt;conclusion&gt;
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.16.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> Skin Yard was from the U.S. (Seattle, Washington). Ostava was from Bulgaria (not the U.S.).
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.16.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
</span></span>&lt;/conclusion&gt;</span><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.16.2" class="ltx_text"></span></span>
<span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.17" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.17.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Action:</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.18" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.18.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="width:384.1pt;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">    stop [Skin Yard was from the U.S. (Seattle, Washington). Ostava was from Bulgaria (not the U.S.).]</span></span>
<span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.19" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.19.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">Final answer:<span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.19.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Skin Yard was from the U.S. (Seattle, Washington). Ostava was from Bulgaria (not the U.S.).<span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.19.1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span></span>
<span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.20" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.20.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">Ground truth:<span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.20.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> no<span id="A2.SS4.p4.pic1.p7.20.1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></span></span></span>
</span></span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.5 </span>filtering strategy and data ratio</h3>

<div id="A2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We used string matching to filter out RFT data that did not conform to our expected format.
To preserve the original data distribution and mitigate the catastrophic forgetting of answer formatting learned during the SFT stage, we randomly sampled 80% of the SFT data to include in the final dataset used for the second-stage training. To ensure consistency in data volume and proportion between the two stages, we randomly selected 400 NQ samples and 673 HotpotQA samples from the filtered Original RFT data, resulting in a total of 1,073 representative reasoning examples. By combining these 1,073 samples with the 80% subset of SFT data, we obtained the final dataset used for RFT training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.6 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="A2.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During the training phase, we adopt the 5.3K synthesized data for SFT and RFT. Both training and evaluation were conducted on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The SFT stage was performed for 2 epochs with a learning rate of 5e-6, while the RFT stage was also trained for 2 epochs, using a lower learning rate of 1e-6. Model evaluation was conducted on the test or validation sets of six publicly available question answering datasets, covering a diverse range of tasks to systematically assess the model’s generalization ability in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings. The evaluation metrics include EM and LLM-based judgment, providing a comprehensive reflection of the model’s accuracy and real-world applicability.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A2.SS7.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.7.2 </span>TriviaQA Results</h4>

<div id="A2.SS7.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS7.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in the Table <a href="#A2.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ B.7.2 TriviaQA Results ‣ B.7 Experimental Results ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, there is a significant discrepancy between the EM scores and LLM-judge evaluation scores for our two models on the TriviaQA dataset. We attribute this gap to the absence of format-specific supervision signals in our training process, which leads to answers that are factually correct but fail to satisfy exact match criteria due to formatting issues. For detailed examples, please refer to the case study in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Case Study ‣ Appendix B Appendix ‣ BrowserAgent: Building Web Agents with Human-Inspired Web Browsing Actions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>

      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
